client: I've been really struggling lately because I missed the deadline for my final project at university, and now I just can't stop thinking about how badly it's going to hurt my grade. The anxiety is constant — like this low hum in the background that spikes whenever I even think about checking my email or logging into the student portal. Honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to fix anything, because the damage is already done, you know?
therapist: It makes complete sense that you're carrying this heavy, constant anxiety — missing a deadline feels like a real loss of control, and that low hum you're describing sounds genuinely exhausting. I also hear a bit of hopelessness in "the damage is already done," and I want to gently explore that thought with you, because our minds often present worst-case scenarios as certainties when we're stressed. What do you imagine is the *most likely* outcome here, versus the absolute worst-case one your mind keeps returning to?

client: Okay, so the worst case my brain keeps going to is that I fail the whole course, lose my scholarship, and basically have to drop out — like one missed deadline becomes this domino effect that ruins everything. The most likely outcome is probably just a significant grade penalty, maybe failing that specific assignment, which would hurt my GPA but not necessarily end everything. But here's the thing — even saying "most likely" out loud doesn't actually make me feel better, because my brain just immediately jumps back to "but what if it IS the worst case?"
therapist: You've just done something really important — you were able to separate the catastrophic story from the more realistic one, even if your feelings haven't caught up yet, and that gap between *knowing* and *feeling* is completely normal and very human. That "but what if" pull is what we call catastrophic thinking, and it's your brain trying to protect you by preparing for danger, even when the danger is unlikely. I'm curious — if a close friend came to you in this exact situation, would you let them spiral into the worst-case domino story, or would you gently point them back to what's most likely true?

client: I'd obviously tell a friend to calm down and that one missed deadline doesn't define their whole future — I can see that clearly when it's someone else. But when it's me, it just feels different, like the rules don't apply the same way, and I know that probably sounds irrational but I can't help it. I guess I'm also a bit skeptical of that whole "talk to yourself like a friend" thing because it feels kind of forced, like I'd just be lying to myself to feel better temporarily.
therapist: You're not being irrational at all — it's actually incredibly common to have more compassion for others than ourselves, and noticing that double standard is a really meaningful insight. I also want to address your skepticism directly, because it's a fair one: the goal isn't to paste positive thoughts over real fears like a Band-Aid, but to ask whether the harsh version you're telling yourself is actually *more* accurate than the kinder one, or just more familiar. When you tell yourself this one deadline could end everything, what evidence do you actually have that supports that, versus evidence that contradicts it?

client: Okay, so evidence that supports the worst case... I mean, I don't actually have any concrete proof that I'll lose my scholarship over this one thing, and I've done well in other assignments this semester. The evidence against it is actually stronger when I think about it — I have a decent overall grade going in, and I've never failed a course before. But I guess what I'm realizing is that even when I lay it out like that, there's this voice that says "yeah but this time is different," and I don't really know how to shut that voice up even when logic is pointing the other way.
therapist: You've just done something genuinely hard — you examined the evidence honestly and found that reality is actually on your side, and that takes real courage when anxiety is loud. That "this time is different" voice doesn't need to be *silenced* so much as recognized for what it is: a familiar protective habit your brain has, not a reliable source of truth. What do you think that voice is most afraid of, underneath all the catastrophizing — is it really about the grade, or is there something deeper it's trying to protect you from?

client: Honestly, when I sit with that question, I think it's less about the grade and more about this fear that I'm not actually as capable as people think I am — like this deadline is proof that I'm falling apart and eventually everyone will see it. There's this constant pressure I put on myself to have everything together, especially at university, because it feels like that's the one area where I've always been able to prove my worth. I don't know, that's kind of uncomfortable to say out loud, and I'm not sure digging into that is going to help me figure out what to actually do about the situation right now.
therapist: What you just shared takes real courage, and I want you to know that discomfort you're feeling is often a sign that we've touched something genuinely important — this idea that your worth depends on always having it together is a heavy thing to carry, and it makes so much sense that one missed deadline would feel catastrophic through that lens. You're right that we also want to think about practical next steps, and I don't think we have to choose between the two — in fact, understanding that this fear is driving the anxiety might actually make it *easier* to take action rather than freeze. Before we think about what to do next practically, I'm wondering: have you actually reached out to your professor yet, and what's been stopping you?

client: No, I haven't reached out, and every time I think about doing it I just... freeze. I think what's stopping me is that sending that email makes it real and official, and there's also this shame around having to explain myself — like admitting I missed it feels like confirming that I'm not as capable as I should be. I know logically that emailing is probably the right move, but I'm honestly not convinced my professor is going to be sympathetic, and I don't want to put myself out there and get a cold response that makes me feel even worse.
therapist: That freezing makes complete sense now — reaching out isn't just a practical step for you, it's emotionally loaded because it feels like handing someone evidence against you, and that's a really vulnerable place to be. But I want to gently offer another way to look at it: most professors have seen students struggle, and reaching out actually tends to signal responsibility and self-awareness rather than incompetence — it's avoidance, not the email, that usually confirms our worst fears to ourselves. What would feel like the smallest, most manageable version of that first step — even just opening a draft without sending it — that might help you test whether the freeze is protecting you or keeping you stuck?

client: I guess I could try just opening a draft, that feels slightly less terrifying than actually sending something. But I'm already anticipating that I'll write it and then just stare at it for days without sending it, which is kind of what happens with things I'm avoiding — I get partway there and then get stuck in this loop. I suppose the honest obstacle is that even a draft feels like it's one step away from the moment where I have to actually be vulnerable, and I'm not sure I'm ready for that.
therapist: That self-awareness is really valuable — you're not just avoiding the email, you're recognizing the *pattern* of getting close and then stalling, which means you already understand yourself better than you might give yourself credit for. That stalling point is actually where the real work is, and it's worth naming that the vulnerability you're dreading — being seen as imperfect — is something you've already done here today with me, and you survived it. I'm wondering, what would it mean about you if you sent that email and your professor *was* understanding — would that be allowed to count as evidence that you're more capable than that fearful voice believes?

client: That's actually a really uncomfortable question because my instinct is to say "yes, of course it would count," but I know deep down I'd probably find a way to dismiss it — like tell myself the professor was just being polite or that it doesn't really prove anything. I think I have this habit of only letting negative evidence stick while finding reasons to reject the positive stuff, and hearing you name that makes me feel kind of exhausted by my own brain. I guess I'm willing to try the draft, but I'm genuinely worried I'll do exactly what I just described — explain away any good outcome so it doesn't actually change how I feel about myself.
therapist: What you just identified — letting negative evidence stick while deflecting the positive — is actually a well-recognized pattern called a mental filter, and the fact that you can see it so clearly in yourself is genuinely significant, even if it feels exhausting right now. That exhaustion you're feeling? It makes complete sense, because running that filtering system takes enormous energy, and you've been doing it for a long time. I'd love to try something small with you: when you write that draft, what if you also jotted down one thing that went *okay* today — not perfectly, just okay — and practiced letting it count, just as an experiment in catching the filter in action?

client: I hear what you're saying, and I'm willing to try it, but I'm already a bit skeptical because writing down "one thing that went okay" feels almost too small to matter when there's this big looming deadline situation hanging over everything. Like, I'm worried it'll feel trivial or performative, and I'll just roll my eyes at myself while doing it. I guess the honest question I have is — does this actually work for people, or does it just feel like busywork that distracts from the real problem?
therapist: Your skepticism is completely valid, and I'd rather you bring that honesty here than force yourself through something that feels hollow — the goal was never to distract you from the real problem, but to gently start loosening the grip of a filtering system that's been making it harder for you to act. What the research does show is that it's less about the exercise itself and more about building the habit of *noticing* when your brain is being a selective editor, so that over time you have a little more choice in what you let land. So rather than the gratitude-journal version that might make you roll your eyes, what would feel like a more honest, less performative way for you to start catching that filter — something that fits how your brain actually works?

client: Maybe something like... when I notice myself dismissing something good, I just mentally call it out in the moment — like "there goes the filter" — without having to write anything down or make it into a whole ritual. That feels more like how my brain actually works, because I'm already pretty analytical and self-aware, so maybe I can use that against the pattern instead of fighting it. I'm still not fully convinced it'll change how I feel about the deadline situation, but I guess it's at least honest rather than forced.
therapist: That's actually a really elegant adaptation — you've taken the idea and shaped it into something that genuinely fits you, and that kind of ownership is exactly what makes these things stick rather than fade. You're right that your analytical nature is an asset here, and "there goes the filter" is a perfect use of it — you're not trying to force positivity, you're just becoming a more accurate observer of your own mind. So you've got two small, honest experiments to try: opening that draft, and catching the filter when it shows up — how are you feeling about those as a starting point, compared to where you were when we began talking?
